title: Relativity made simple
examples: If I travel very fast, will my clock tick slower?
How does the speed of light being constant help us understand the universe?

explain.say: Today we explore special relativity concepts. We will start with the constancy of the speed of light.

items: The speed of light in a vacuum is always c.
This speed is about three times ten to the eight meters per second.
It does not depend on the motion of the source or observer.

draw.text: Speed of light is constant for all observers.

explain.say: Next we look at the implications for distance and time. These measurements change depending on your speed.

draw.text: Length and time change with speed.

explain.say: This brings us to time dilation. Time appears to pass slower for a moving object.
The formula shows time passing slower by the Lorentz factor. This factor depends on speed.
Consider a muon, a particle created high in the atmosphere. It travels very fast toward Earth.
In everyday life, this effect is measured by GPS satellites. They experience time dilation relative to Earth.

draw.text: GPS clocks must correct for time dilation.

faq.q: If time slows down for me, does it mean I am moving slower?
faq.a: No, it means that relative to someone else, time passes slower for you. You feel time passing normally to yourself.
asks: Does moving slow down my clock?
Is my time ticking slower for others?

faq.q: Does gravity also cause time to change?
faq.a: Yes, general relativity shows that gravity affects the passage of time. Time runs slower in stronger gravitational fields.

faq.q: Why is the speed of light always constant?
faq.a: This is a fundamental postulate of special relativity. It means all observers measure the speed of light as exactly the same value.
asks: Why can't I measure different speeds of light?
Is c always the same speed?

faq.q: How much time does it slow down at near light speed?
faq.a: The slowing effect becomes very pronounced as your speed approaches the speed of light. It approaches zero only at exactly the speed of light.
asks: How fast do I need to go to notice time change?
Is the time dilation effect small at moderate speeds?

faq.q: Is this only theoretical, or is it proven?
faq.a: It is strongly supported by experiments, like those involving particle decay and GPS accuracy. These effects are measurable.
asks: Are these theories just math problems?
Can we prove time dilation in a lab?

facts: The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 meters per second.
Time dilation predicts that moving clocks run slower when measured by a stationary observer.
The effect of time dilation is negligible at everyday speeds like a car trip.
The Lorentz factor determines the degree of time slowing observed.
